title: Managing multidrug resistant Gram-negative bacteraemia in immunocompromised hosts
one_line_summary: Management of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bloodstream infections in immunocompromised hosts requires risk-stratified empirical therapy, integration of rapid diagnostics, pharmacokinetically optimized targeted regimens, and structured antimicrobial stewardship.
key_pearls: - In solid organ transplant (**SOT**) recipients, **MDR** Gram-negative bacteria cause **19% to 40%** of bloodstream infections (**BSI**), with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (**CRE**) driving **30-day** **mortality** rates of **33% to 66%** (*aHR 2.85*).

- In patients with haematological malignancies (**HM**), **30-day** **mortality** for **MDR** Gram-negative **BSI** reaches **27% to 34%** compared to **7% to 8%** in non-**MDR** cases (*OR 5.02*), with peak **mortality** in **CRAB** (**56%**) and **MBL**-producing **K. pneumoniae** (**47–55%**).

- Prior rectal colonization with **CRE** exhibits a positive predictive value of approximately **50%** for invasive infection; empirical coverage in stable carriers should incorporate secondary risk factors like multisite colonization.

- Continuous or extended infusions of novel **β-lactams** combined with therapeutic drug monitoring (**TDM**) optimize pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (**PK/PD**) targets and mitigate resistance selection caused by **β-lactamase inhibitor** exposure mismatch.

- Presence of **MDR** status alone does not justify extending antibiotic treatment duration beyond **7 days** in clinically stable patients who have achieved rapid microbiological clearance and source control.
population: Immunocompromised hosts, specifically solid organ transplant (SOT) recipients and patients with haematological malignancies (HM) or undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT)

sections.heading: Epidemiology and MDR Burden
sections.content:
- Gram-negative bacteria cause **6% to 20%** of **BSIs** within the first post-transplant year in **SOT** recipients, with liver transplant recipients experiencing the highest incidence (**12.3%** vs **2.6%** in kidney transplants).
- Predominant pathogens in **SOT** hosts include **Escherichia coli** (**29–64%**), **Klebsiella pneumoniae** (**10–42%**), **Pseudomonas aeruginosa** (**10–34%**), and **Acinetobacter baumannii** (**8–20%**).
- In patients with **HM**, Gram-negative organisms account for **42% to 63%** of all **BSI** episodes, with cumulative **30-day** post-allogeneic **HSCT** incidence reaching **17.3%**.
- Extended-spectrum cephalosporin resistance (**ESCR-E**) affects **15–45%** of Enterobacterales **BSIs** in **SOT** and **17–66%** in **HM**; **CRE** rates range from **8–22%** in **SOT** to **13–39%** in **HM**.
- In **HM** patients, **BSIs** occurring **>= 30 days** post-**HSCT** independently predict markedly higher **mortality** (*OR 11.21*).
section_pearls: Liver transplant recipients have the highest rate of post-transplant Gram-negative BSI among SOT recipients.
MDR status increases 30-day BSI mortality over four-fold in patients with haematological malignancies.

sections.heading: Empirical Therapy and Colonization Screening
sections.content:
- Empirical regimens depend on clinical severity (**SOFA** / **qSOFA** scores), local epidemiology, and previous host colonization status.
- In **ESCR-E** high-prevalence settings, carbapenems remain first-line, but carbapenem-sparing agents such as **piperacillin-tazobactam** or **cefepime-enmetazobactam** can be used in stable urinary-source **BSIs**.
- Sparing antianaerobic antibiotics (e.g. **piperacillin-tazobactam**, carbapenems) in **allo-HSCT** or **CAR-T** recipients preserves gut microbiome diversity and may decrease graft-versus-host disease (**GVHD**) and severe cytokine release syndrome (**CRS**).
- Systematic rectal screening for **MDR-GN** carriage has a positive predictive value (**PPV**) of ~**50%**; empirical escalation should consider multisite colonization or complicated post-transplant courses.
- European Conference on Infections in Leukaemia (**ECIL**) guidelines recommend empirical novel **β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor** (**BL/BLI**) combinations for neutropenic patients at high risk for **CPE** or difficult-to-treat **P. aeruginosa**.

sections.heading: Quasi-Targeted Therapy and Rapid Diagnostics
sections.content:
- Molecular rapid diagnostic testing provides prompt genotypic resistance identification, but preliminary negative results should guide antimicrobial escalation rather than de-escalation in **SOT** recipients due to unmapped resistance mechanisms.
- Unmeasured phenotypic resistance mechanisms (e.g., specific **KPC** variants like **KPC-31** causing variable **ceftazidime-avibactam** susceptibility) require caution when relying purely on genotypic detection.
- Machine-learning risk models integrating **MALDI-TOF** mass spectrometry identification, clinical parameters, and colonization history can accurately predict resistance profiles at early diagnosis.

sections.heading: Targeted Therapy and PK/PD Optimization
sections.content:
- Targeted treatment for **CRE** and difficult-to-treat **P. aeruginosa** centers on novel **BL/BLIs** (e.g., **ceftazidime-avibactam**) and **cefiderocol**.
- Combination therapy for **P. aeruginosa** **BSI** is favored in haematological malignancy patients presenting with **critical** illness or pulmonary infection sources.
- Continuous or extended infusion schedules of novel **β-lactams** enhance pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (**PK/PD**) target attainment and clinical response in **critically** ill liver transplant recipients.
- Therapeutic drug monitoring (**TDM**) corrects pharmacokinetic mismatch between **β-lactam** and **β-lactamase inhibitor** components (e.g. **avibactam**), preventing resistance selection driven by inadequate inhibitor concentrations.

sections.heading: Stewardship, Duration, and Follow-Up Blood Cultures
sections.content:
- Oral step-down therapy is effective for stable non-**MDR** Gram-negative **BSIs**, but oral options for **MDR-GNB** remain extremely limited.
- **MDR** status alone is not an indication for prolonged intravenous therapy; randomized trial evidence supports **7-day** versus **14-day** courses in uncomplicated Gram-negative **BSIs**.
- Routine follow-up blood cultures (**FUBCs**) have low microbiological yield and increase false-positive contaminant risks, but remain useful in high-risk hosts when persistent endovascular infection or uncontrolled sources are suspected.
- Implementing a structured Gram-negative **BSI** management bundle reduces new **MDR-GN** colonization and secondary hospital-acquired infections.

strengths_limitations:
- **Strengths**: Comprehensive synthesis of recent epidemiological and management data tailored to specific immunocompromised host populations (**SOT** and **HM**); incorporates modern strategies including rapid molecular diagnostics, machine learning, **PK/PD** dosing, and stewardship bundles.
- **Limitations**: Narrative review design without formal systematic meta-analytic pooling; heavy reliance on observational retrospective cohorts subject to selection and immortal-time biases; sparse randomized controlled trial data specifically evaluating novel **BL/BLIs** in transplant subgroups.

drugs_doses.dose: 2.5 g IV q8h (infused over 2-3h or continuous infusion), adjusted for renal clearance
drugs_doses.indication: Targeted therapy for carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) and KPC-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream infections
drugs_doses.adverse_effects: Development of resistance via KPC point mutations (e.g. KPC-31), renal elimination mismatch requiring TDM monitoring

drugs_doses.dose: 2 g IV q8h (infused over 3h), adjusted for renal clearance
drugs_doses.indication: Targeted therapy for carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacteria including metallo-beta-lactamase (MBL) producers, CRAB, and CRPA
drugs_doses.adverse_effects: Transaminase elevations, gastrointestinal intolerance, resistance emergence

drugs_doses.indication: Carbapenem-sparing therapy for extended-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (ESCR-E) infections
drugs_doses.adverse_effects: Cefepime-associated neurotoxicity risk in renal impairment, rash, diarrhea

drugs_doses.indication: Empirical or carbapenem-sparing targeted therapy for susceptible Gram-negative BSI from urinary sources
drugs_doses.adverse_effects: Gut microbiome depletion, increased risk of GVHD in allo-HSCT recipients, synergistic nephrotoxicity with vancomycin

drugs_doses.dose: 100 mg IV loading dose, then 50 mg IV q12h
drugs_doses.indication: Combination therapy for carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative organ preservation solution contamination or invasive soft tissue/abdominal infections
drugs_doses.adverse_effects: Suboptimal serum/bloodstream levels for primary bacteremia, severe nausea/vomiting, increased mortality risk in severe sepsis
